name: Institution
notes:
Closure recorded from a primary news source. Abraham Lincoln's Namesake College Set to Close After 157 Years
Lincoln College Will Close in May Without Gift to Overcome COVID-19 Impact

 

LINCOLN, IL — Lincoln College has notified the Illinois Department of Higher Education and Higher Learning Commission of permanent closure, effective May 13, 2022. The Board of Trustees has voted to cease all academic programming at the end of the spring semester.

 

Lincoln College has survived many difficult and challenging times – the economic crisis of 1887, a major campus fire in 1912, the Spanish flu of 1918, the Great Depression, World War II, the 2008 global financial crisis, and more, but this is different. Lincoln College needs help to survive.

 

The institution experienced record-breaking student enrollment in Fall 2019, with residence halls at maximum capacity. Unfortunately, the coronavirus pandemic dramatically impacted recruitment and fundraising efforts, sporting events, and all campus life activities. The economic burdens initiated by the pandemic required large investments in technology and campus safety measures, as well as a significant drop in enrollment with students choosing to postpone college or take a leave of absence, which impacted the institution’s financial position.

 

Furthermore, Lincoln College was a victim of a cyberattack in December 2021 that thwarted admissions activities and hindered access to all institutional data, creating an unclear picture of Fall 2022 enrollment projections. All systems required for recruitment, retention, and fundraising efforts were inoperable. Fortunately, no personal identifying information was exposed. Once fully restored in March 2022, the projections displayed significant enrollment shortfalls, requiring a transformational donation or partnership to sustain Lincoln College beyond the current semester.

“Lincoln College has been serving students from across the globe for more than 157 years,” said David Gerlach, president of Lincoln College. “The loss of history, careers, and a community of students and alumni is immense.”

The institution has worked tirelessly to strengthen its financial position through fundraising campaigns, selling assets, consolidating employee positions, and exploring alternatives for the leased building in Normal. Unfortunately, these efforts did not create long-term viability for Lincoln College in the face of the pandemic.

 

Lincoln College encourages individuals to review the FAQ documents on the Lincoln College website for more information regarding the closure process. Academic support and transitional services will be available to students through the remainder of the semester.

“Though we are experiencing undeniable grief and sadness, we find comfort in knowing Lincoln College has served generations of alumni who have undoubtedly impacted our world.”

name: The College of Saint Rose
notes:
Closure recorded from a primary news source. The College of St. Rose to Close at the End of the Spring 2024 Semester!
December 5, 2023


Dear Commons Community

The College of Saint Rose, a Roman Catholic institution in Albany, N.Y., will close its doors at the end of the spring semester, following years of declining enrollment and labor battles. The institution’s board voted on the closure last week. The president, Marcia J. White, called the decision “truly heartbreaking” in her announcement to the campus community on Friday.

Saint Rose, which was founded in 1920 and enrolled nearly 2,800 students in the fall of 2022, according to federal data, has endured years of financial hardship, which came to a head this week when it asked the City of Albany, Albany County, and the State of New York for emergency funding, as the Albany Times Union reported. None of those entities were able to provide an immediate bailout, leading the college’s board to call it quits.

Here are further details as provided by The Daily Gazette and The Albany Times Union.

After news organizations broke the news Thursday afternoon that The College of Saint Rose will close next year, President Marcia White was met Friday with boos, and angry students and staff while explaining why the school will permanently close in May.

The announcement with students and staff was held at the Massry Center for the Arts, but ahead of the speech, some would-be attendees were told they could not enter as the 405-seat hall was at maximum capacity. One staff member said they were not expecting so many people to show up. They scrambled to set up speakers outside in the hall for the leftover people who were not allowed in, as they did, one student commented, “They couldn’t even get this right.”

The College of Saint Rose’s Board of Trustees voted to close the school on Thursday. The college’s Board of Trustees Chair Jeffrey Stone kicked off the announcement on Friday, saying cost-cutting and fundraising efforts by the college were not enough to bridge the financial gap the institution faces.

“As it became more clear that the college would be unable to continue as a standalone institution, we sought financial support from the legislature and other elected officials and, behind the scenes, actively sought to partner with a like-minded institution of higher learning to continue our 103 years. But, those efforts were unsuccessful. The board’s decision to close The College of Saint Rose was not an easy one,” Stone said.

Only a few minutes into his speech, he was met with booing from the crowd. When White interjected to tell students to be more respectful, the crowd both inside and outside the hall only voiced their anger louder.

White spoke after and said she wanted to address what she called factual errors and misinformation in media reports of the closure. Earlier last week, the Albany Times Union reported that the school was facing mounting debt and had lobbied state officials for emergency funds.

“It was reported that we recently reached out to various political leaders for a financial bailout. That is not true. We never asked for a bailout. That was not a request for immediate funding,” White said. “It was a request for bridge funding to support operations through the 2024-2025 academic year to give us time to work towards a continuation of the college’s critical programs to a potential partnership with another institution and to the programs that significantly increase the professional workforce in fields that are facing a shortage of crisis proportion in New York State.”

Speaking to reporters following the community gathering, White criticized reporters for breaking the news of the college’s closing.

“The only reason that I’m not a wreck and in tears is I am so angry at the fact that our students, our faculty, our employees, their parents, the parents of our students had to hear this news in the press, rather than from us today, which is a time we had put aside to do a personal message to them and have a conversation,” she said.

She also reiterated that the request for state funding was not a “bailout,” but a request for “bridge funding.”

White said the college had been in financial trouble for about 10 years and there was a decline in enrollment that was exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic. She said, during that time, the school cut $9 million in administrative costs and $6 million in academic programs, while also looking for potential partnerships. She said the school signed non-disclosure agreements, so she could not share which institutions were approached. It is also unclear how big a budget gap the school faces.

Another question is what will happen to the college’s 48-acre campus in the city’s Pine Hills neighborhood. In a joint statement, Albany Mayor Kathy Sheehan and Albany County Executive Dan McCoy expressed their sadness for the students and staff.

“We are in close communication with City and County stakeholders, state and local government leaders, academia, and developers to ensure that we are all working together to reimagine the CSR campus to minimize the impact of the College’s closure,” the statement read. “In the coming weeks and months, we will also work with the College’s staff to connect them to job opportunities with the City, County, and other local employers through job fairs and other events.”

Sad news for the College’s students, faculty, and staff and the City of Albany!

Tony

notes:
Merger/consolidation recorded from a primary source. OAKLAND CITY, Ind. (WFIE) - Oakland City University is getting rid of some of their employees.

OCU spokesperson Todd Mosby says they are suspending their undergraduate programs and laying off employees.

The layoffs are effective at the end of the month, May 31st.

We’re told students will be provided guidance and options for next steps as plans move forward.

“OCU will continue to offer graduate-level programs and prepare to resume undergraduate operations in the 2027–28 academic year," says Mosby.

This comes as more than 100 employees tell us they still have not received their paycheck.

[READ MORE: Another day with no pay for OCU employees]

Last week, OCU administration held a series of meetings with employees, where they announced the university’s plans to stay open.

[PREVIOUS: OCU to stay open for now, employees still waiting to be paid]

Mosby said last week the university finalized a “strategic partnership” that should allow them to keep operations running.

Mosby was unable to discuss specifics on the partnership with us, saying the details still had to be signed onto paper.

We have learned the deal has not gone through yet.

We are closely following this story and will have further updates in our newscasts tonight on 14 News.

Students received this letter from OCU Tuesday afternoon:

“Dear Students,

After much prayer, thoughtful consideration, and careful evaluation of the current financial realities facing our institution, we are writing to inform you that undergraduate academic programs will be suspended for the 2026–2027 academic year. We understand this announcement will bring disappointment, uncertainty, and many questions. Please know that our commitment to you remains strong, and our immediate focus is helping every student determine the best path forward. We do believe that within the next year, our carbon capture patent will be sold, and we will reopen in the fall of 2027.

Your administration, deans, advisors, and coaches stand ready to assist you in your next steps.

1. Students Within 25 Credit Hours of Graduation

Students who are within 25 credit hours of completing their degree should contact their major advisor or school dean to discuss possible teach-out opportunities that may allow them to complete their program requirements during Fall 26 and Spring 27.

2. Transfer to Another Institution

Students who wish to continue their education uninterrupted are encouraged to work closely with their dean, advisor, or athletic coach regarding transfer opportunities to another institution. We are committed to assisting students in making this transition as smooth as possible. Since most of our students are student-athletes, you will want to transfer and play sports at another institution. Please work closely with your coach.

OCU has signed an agreement with the University of Southern Indiana which will allow students to transfer to USI. We appreciate USI for graciously working with us and you. If you are interested in this options, please visit https://www.usi.edu/admissions/transfer-students

3. Take a Temporary Leave and Return in Fall 2027

We are confident that the OCU undergraduate programs will return in Fall 2027. Therefore, students may choose to pause their college studies for the 2026–2027 academic year and plan to return when undergraduate programs resume in Fall 2027.

While such a decision presents significant challenges, we remain confident in God’s faithfulness and guidance for Oakland City University and for each of you individually. Your education, calling, and future matter deeply to us, and we are committed to walking alongside you through these next steps.

Please continue to pray for wisdom, unity, and clarity for our entire college community.

Sincerely,

Ron D. Dempsey

President

Oakland City University

name: Rosemont College
notes:
Announced closure recorded from a primary news source; not yet closed. Villanova, a significantly larger institution, will absorb Rosemont, which is located less than a mile away. The deal looks more like an acquisition versus a merger and comes as Rosemont has struggled financially and with enrollment, leaning heavily in its endowment to stay afloat. The small college, located less than a mile from Villanova, will be renamed Villanova University, Rosemont Campus, in a move that seems more akin to an acquisition than a merger. Tenured and tenure-track faculty at Rosemont will reportedly be offered teaching contacts.

Like many small colleges, Rosemont has faced financial and enrollment challenges recently. Rosemont’s enrollment stood at 777 students in fall 2023, according to recent federal data. While that number was higher than the two preceding years, it fell short of the 902 students Rosemont enrolled in 2019, or in previous years when the college typically surpassed the 1,000 mark.

Public financial records show that Rosemont operated at a loss in the last four fiscal years. Amid the financial struggles, Rosemont has borrowed $7 million from its endowment—recently valued at $23 million—since 2020. A recent audit indicated “substantial doubt” that Rosemont would be able to remain open if its financial struggles persisted.

During the merger process—which is expected to be completed in 2028, pending regulatory approvals—Rosemont will stay open and operate independently, with financial support from Villanova. But officials told the Inquirer they will stop accepting new students in October.

The Rosemont merger comes after Cabrini University, another small private college in the Philadelphia region, closed in May 2024. Villanova purchased Cabrini’s campus soon afterward.

Financial challenges have battered colleges in the Keystone State in recent years, with three institutions announcing closures last year. Another, the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts, ended its degree programs but remains open as a museum. More closures are on the horizon as Pennsylvania State University considers a plan to shutter up to 12 of its campuses.

name: Arkansas Holiness College
notes: Nazarene college; merged with Bethany-Peniel College in 1931.

name: Bresee Theological College
notes: Nazarene junior college (orig. Kansas Holiness Bible College, 1905); financially overwhelmed, it closed to merge into Bethany-Peniel College in 1940.

name: Central Nazarene College
notes: Nazarene junior college; consolidated with Bethany-Peniel College in 1929.

name: Nazarene Bible Institute
notes: Nazarene Bible institute; closed and merged into Central Nazarene College in 1911 amid a denominational realignment.

name: Pentecostal Collegiate Institute (New York)
notes: Holiness-movement institute; closed Feb 1903 after its president incurred unauthorized debt and filed for bankruptcy; an antecedent of Eastern Nazarene College.

name: St. Anthony-on-Hudson Seminary
notes: Franciscan Roman Catholic seminary (1912-1988); closed as part of a national trend toward concentrating seminarians at large centers.

name: Brookwood Labor College
notes: Residential labor college ('labor's Harvard'), 1921-1937; the board voted Nov 21, 1937 to suspend and close amid Depression-era financial pressure. Alumni include Walter Reuther and Ella Baker.

name: Art Institute of Buffalo
notes: Private art school (1931-1956); contracted and closed as the postwar GI Bill enrollment wave receded. Faculty included Charles Burchfield.

name: Barleywood Female University
notes: Short-lived Rochester women's college (1852-1853); fell into debt and closed within a year, its land donated to the University of Rochester.

name: Briarcliff College
notes: Women's college (orig. Mrs. Dow's School, 1903; 4-year from 1957); trustees sold the campus to Pace University in 1977 amid the shift to coeducation. Peak enrollment 623 (1967).

name: Briarcliffe College-Patchogue
notes: Patchogue branch campus (est. 1980) of the for-profit Briarcliffe College; permanently closed in 2018 with its parent.

name: Bennett College (New York)
notes: Women's junior college in Millbrook, NY (1890-1977); closed Aug 9, 1977 after a costly, failed attempt to modernize and go coed. Distinct from Bennett College in Greensboro, NC. Alumni include Ray Eames.

name: Elizabeth Seton College
notes: Catholic two-year women's college (Sisters of Charity of New York); merged into the stronger Iona College in 1989, its Yonkers campus closing in 1995. About 980 students in 1988.

name: Ladycliff College
notes: Catholic college (Franciscan Sisters of Peekskill) adjacent to West Point, 1933-1980; closed after the 1979-80 year, its property acquired by the U.S. Military Academy for its museum.

name: Maria Regina College
notes: Catholic junior college for women, Syracuse (founded c.1934); closed 1990 per Wikipedia, though a cited source gives 1988. No successor named.

name: Marymount College, Tarrytown
notes: Catholic women's college (Religious of the Sacred Heart of Mary, 1907); consolidated into Fordham University in 2000 but closed after the 2007 class, campus sold in 2008 for $27M.

name: St. Pius X Preparatory Seminary
notes: Catholic minor seminary of the Diocese of Rockville Centre (founded 1961); its junior college closed in 1968 and its high school in 1984.

name: New York State College of Forestry at Cornell University
notes: New York's first state forestry college, a public statutory college at Cornell (1898); lost its state appropriation to a gubernatorial pocket veto amid the Adirondack clearcutting controversy and ceased instruction in June 1903. name: Soule College
notes: A Presbyterian college in Dodge City, Kansas that operated 1888-1903; its property later passed to St. Mary of the Plains College.

name: New York Central College
notes: An abolitionist Baptist liberal-arts college in McGrawville, NY (1848); closed in 1860 after a smallpox epidemic combined with financial difficulties and political opposition.

name: Troy University (New York)
notes: A Methodist four-year college in Troy, NY (1858); failed financially in the early 1860s, was foreclosed on, and sent its remaining 13 students to Wesleyan University.

name: Ingham University
notes: A pioneering women's college in Le Roy, NY (chartered as a university 1857, rooted in an 1835 seminary); closed in 1892 after financial difficulties, its property auctioned in 1895.

name: Rutgers Female College
notes: An independent New York City women's college (chartered 1838/founded 1839, unrelated to Rutgers University); ceased operations in 1894.

name: State and National Law School
notes: A law school founded 1849 in Ballston Spa, later Poughkeepsie, NY; closed in 1865 amid Civil War-driven enrollment decline.

name: Genesee Wesleyan Seminary
notes: A Methodist Episcopal seminary in Lima, NY (1831); closed as a seminary in 1941. Its distinct college arm had earlier become the nucleus of Syracuse University.

name: Oneida Institute
notes: An 1827 Presbyterian manual-labor college in Whitesboro, NY, noted for interracial admission and abolitionism; closed in 1843 amid financial failure and hostility, its facilities becoming Whitestown Seminary.

name: Eisenhower College
notes: A private liberal-arts college in Seneca Falls, NY (founded 1965, opened 1968); acquired by RIT in March 1979 and closed by RIT on July 22, 1982 after major operating deficits.

name: Finch College
notes: A private Manhattan women's college founded 1900 (baccalaureate from 1952); closed in 1976 after a small endowment and falling enrollment, records transferred to Marymount Manhattan College.

name: Cathedral College of the Immaculate Conception
notes: A Roman Catholic seminary college founded in Brooklyn in 1914 (restructured as a four-year college seminary in 1967); the college closed in 1987.

name: Harlem Hospital School of Nursing
notes: A public hospital-based nursing diploma school founded Jan 3, 1923, the first nursing school for African-American women in New York City; closed in 1977 partly due to lack of funding.

name: Lincoln School for Nurses
notes: A hospital-based diploma nursing school in the Bronx (1898), the first nursing school for African-American women in New York City; closed September 5, 1961 after 1,864 alumnae.

name: New York Hydropathic and Physiological School
notes: A 19th-century New York City medical/hydropathy school (1853) that conferred the M.D. degree; closed in 1875 when it was offered for sale.

name: King's College (New York City)
notes: A private non-denominational Christian liberal-arts college in New York City (founded 1938; not the colonial Columbia predecessor); did not open for fall 2023 and began dissolution after COVID-era financial difficulties and loss of Middle States accreditation on Aug 31, 2023.

name: Packard Business College
notes: A New York City for-profit business college founded 1858; closed by 1954, after which its building was bought by Stern College for Women.

name: TCI College of Technology
notes: A New York City for-profit two-year college founded 1909 as the Marconi Institute; closed September 1, 2017 citing economic factors.

name: Wood Tobe-Coburn School
notes: A New York City for-profit career college descending from the 1937 Tobe-Coburn School (merged with the Wood School in 1992, renamed 1993); closed in 2017.

name: Traphagen School of Fashion
notes: A New York City fashion and design school founded 1923 by Ethel Traphagen Leigh; closed in 1991 after 68 years.

name: Grand Central School of Art
notes: A New York City art school run by the Grand Central Art Galleries cooperative (1922); closed in 1944 after nearly 20 years. Non-degree.

name: Dramatic Workshop
notes: A New York City acting school founded 1940, initially housed at The New School; sustained by Saul C. Colin until his death in 1967, when it ended. Non-degree; alumni include Marlon Brando and Tennessee Williams.

name: Boykin's School of Art
notes: A non-degree art academy, noted as the first art school for African Americans in New York City when it opened there in 1929; closed in 1935.

name: National Shakespeare Conservatory
notes: A New York City actor-training conservatory founded 1974; lost federal student-aid eligibility in 1996 and fully closed in late 1998.

name: Onondaga School of Therapeutic Massage
notes: A for-profit massage-therapy school with Syracuse and Rochester campuses (1997); closed December 10, 2021.
motto: Change lives. Start with Yours.

name: Granville Female College
notes: A Presbyterian women's college in Granville, Ohio; closed in 1898.

name: Springfield Industrial Institute
notes: A Christian missionary trade school in Springfield, Massachusetts (founded 1887, twice renamed); discontinued in 1898, its building leased to a high school.

name: Kirkland College
notes: A private women's liberal-arts college in Clinton, NY (1965); absorbed by adjacent Hamilton College in 1978 after failing to become economically self-sufficient.

name: Union Graduate College
notes: A graduate-only college in Schenectady, NY (1905, independent from Union College in 2003); merged into Clarkson University Feb 1, 2016 as its Capital Region Campus, both reportedly fiscally sound.

name: Genesee College
notes: A Methodist college in Lima, NY (1850); dissolved by 1875 after its students, faculty, and library moved to Syracuse, becoming the nucleus of Syracuse University, when the railroad bypassed Lima.

name: Geneva Medical College
notes: The Episcopal-affiliated medical department of Hobart College in Geneva, NY (1834), where Elizabeth Blackwell earned the first US medical degree to a woman (1849); discontinued by Hobart in 1872 amid enrollment collapse and transferred to Syracuse University (now SUNY Upstate Medical University).

name: Sage College of Albany
notes: A college in Albany (1949); consolidated in fall 2020 into the still-operating Russell Sage College as its Albany campus amid declining enrollment and a high debt load.

name: College of Insurance
notes: A Manhattan college of insurance (1901); its programs were taken over by St. John's University in 2001, becoming that university's School of Risk Management, Insurance and Actuarial Science.

name: Jewish Institute of Religion
notes: A Reform-Jewish rabbinical seminary founded 1922 in NYC by Rabbi Stephen S. Wise; merged into Hebrew Union College in 1950 amid budgetary difficulties.

name: Notre Dame College (Staten Island)
notes: A Catholic college on Staten Island (1933); consolidated into St. John's University in 1971, becoming its Staten Island Campus, as small colleges struggled in the late 1960s.

name: Columbia University School of Library Service
notes: Columbia's pioneering library school (founded 1887 as the School of Library Economy); closed as a division on June 30, 1992 amid a university budget crisis, while Columbia continues.

name: Theological School of St. Lawrence University
notes: The Universalist seminary at St. Lawrence University (1856); closed in 1965 after its sponsoring denomination merged into the Unitarian Universalist Association, while the parent university continues.

name: Schools of Public Engagement
notes: A degree-granting division of the still-operating New School (1919); its programs were absorbed into other New School divisions in 2025-26 under a university-wide restructuring.

name: Marymount College (Kansas)
notes: A Roman Catholic four-year college in Salina, Kansas (Sisters of St. Joseph of Concordia), founded 1922; closed in June 1989, its campus becoming the Kansas Highway Patrol Training Center.

name: Westmar University
notes: A four-year Methodist-lineage college in Le Mars, Iowa, founded 1887; closed November 21, 1997 after failing to find a merger partner.

name: Baltimore Female College
notes: The first institution of higher learning for women in Maryland, a Methodist women's college founded 1849 in Baltimore; closed in 1890.

name: Maryland College for Women
notes: A Lutheran women's college in Lutherville, Maryland (founded 1853 as the Lutherville Female Seminary, renamed 1895); closed in 1952, the property becoming a senior citizens' home.

name: Kee Mar College
notes: A Lutheran women's degree-granting college in Hagerstown, Maryland (founded 1853 as the Hagerstown Female Seminary, renamed 1889); closed in 1911 after financial trouble.

name: Norfolk College for Young Ladies
notes: A private women's college chartered Feb. 20, 1880 in Norfolk, Virginia; closed by 1899 when Mary Washington College took over its building.

name: Sullins College
notes: A Methodist two-year women's junior college in Bristol, Virginia (1870); ceased operations in 1976 amid declining enrollment and debt.

name: Wesleyan Female College (Wilmington)
notes: A Methodist women's college in Wilmington, Delaware (founded 1837); closed in 1885 after enrollment declined through the 1870s and an 1880 smallpox outbreak.

name: Judson College (Mount Palatine, Illinois)
notes: A Baptist college in Mount Palatine, Illinois (1846); lost enrollment after a railroad bypassed it and was sold under fiscal duress by the sheriff in 1860. Unrelated to present-day Judson University in Elgin.

name: Aquinas College (Massachusetts)
notes: A private Catholic women's college in Milton and Newton, Massachusetts (founded 1956); closed in 2000, its records held at Regis College.

name: Bradford College (United States)
notes: A private college in Haverhill, Massachusetts (founded 1803; a junior college from 1932, four-year from 1971); closed in May 2000 amid budget shortfalls of over $1M and declining enrollment.
motto: Surgo ut Prosim

name: Cardinal Cushing College
notes: A Catholic women's college in Brookline, Massachusetts, sponsored by the Sisters of the Holy Cross (founded 1952); closed in 1972.

name: Oread Institute
notes: An early women's institute in Worcester, Massachusetts (founded 1849) offering a college-level curriculum; closed as an institution in 1881.

name: Lone Mountain College
notes: A private Catholic college founded 1898 (Religious of the Sacred Heart); acquired by the University of San Francisco in 1978 to become USF's Lone Mountain Campus.

name: Mount Saint Agnes College
notes: A Catholic women's college run by the Sisters of Mercy in Baltimore (founded 1890); merged into Loyola College in Maryland in 1971 and ceased as its own degree-granting institution in 1972.

name: Bible Normal College
notes: A non-denominational Bible and teacher-training school (founded 1885 in Springfield, MA; moved to Hartford, CT in 1897); merged with two other schools in 1961 to form the Hartford Seminary Foundation.

name: Newton College of the Sacred Heart
notes: A Catholic women's college run by the Society of the Sacred Heart in Newton, Massachusetts (founded 1946); merged into Boston College in 1974 amid declining enrollment and financial pressure.
motto: Caritas Christi Urget Nos: The love of Christ compels us

name: Cascade College
notes: A Churches-of-Christ college in Portland, Oregon (founded 1956 as Columbia Christian College, renamed Cascade College when Oklahoma Christian University adopted it as a branch in 1994); closed by that parent at the end of the 2009 academic year for financial reasons.

name: St. Thomas Seminary (Denver)
notes: Roman Catholic major seminary run by the Congregation of the Mission (Vincentians). Founded 1908; closed 1995 amid falling enrollment.

name: St. Joseph's Seminary (Washington, D.C.)
notes: Josephite major seminary; founded 1888 in Baltimore, relocated to Washington, D.C. in 1930. Closed for studies in the early 1970s (no exact year in the cited source).

name: St. Joseph College Seminary (Illinois)
notes: College seminary of the Archdiocese of Chicago for college-aged men; founded 1964 as Saint Mary's College. Closed June 2019 in an archdiocesan consolidation.

name: Tolentine College
notes: Augustinian college and seminary; founded 1958. Theology division closed 1968; college seminarians transferred to Villanova in 1973; closed 1974 citing financial issues.

name: St. Charles Seminary (Ohio)
notes: Theologate of the Missionaries of the Precious Blood in Carthagena, Ohio; founded 1861. Closed 1969 amid declining enrollment; theology students moved to Catholic Theological Union, Chicago. Distinct from the operating St. Charles Borromeo Seminary in Pennsylvania.

name: St. John's Provincial Seminary
notes: Major seminary of the Archdiocese of Detroit; operated 1949 to 1988 (closed June 7, 1988). Cause of closure not stated in the cited source.

name: St. Vincent's Seminary (Missouri)
notes: Vincentian college and seminary; founded 1838. Closed 1979; grounds became the River Campus of Southeast Missouri State University. Cause not stated in the cited source.

name: Mount St. Alphonsus Seminary
notes: Redemptorist theologate; founded 1907. Seminarians relocated to Washington Theological Union in 1985 amid declining numbers; the facility finally closed January 1, 2012.

name: Mary Immaculate Seminary
notes: Vincentian major seminary; founded 1939. The last class graduated in 1990 amid declining vocations.

name: St. Mary's College (Kentucky)
notes: Catholic men's college near Lebanon, Kentucky; operated 1821 to 1976. Cause of closure not stated in the cited source.

name: Annhurst College
notes: Catholic college founded 1941 by the Daughters of the Holy Spirit; opened as a junior college, became four-year in 1943. Closed May 1980 under mounting debt.
motto: Deus Primus Serviatur: God First Served

name: College of Saint Teresa
notes: Catholic women's college founded 1907 by the Sisters of Saint Francis of Rochester, Minnesota. Closed 1989 amid declining enrollment.

name: St. John's College (Kansas)
notes: Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod junior college in Winfield, Kansas; founded 1893. Closed at the end of the spring 1986 semester as the LCMS consolidated its schools.

name: Bethel Bible College
notes: Charles Parham's Bible school, founded 1900 in Topeka and remembered as a birthplace of Pentecostalism. Closed 1901 after a fire destroyed the building.

name: College of the Sisters of Bethany
notes: Episcopal Diocese of Kansas school in Topeka; operated from 1861 until 1928. The cited source is a stub and states neither the level nor the cause of closure.

name: Concordia Normal School
notes: Kansas state normal school (teacher training); founded 1874. Closed March 18, 1878 as state normal-school funding was consolidated to what is now Emporia State University. The cited source's lead gives 1876 while its body gives March 1878.

name: Great Western Business and Normal College
notes: Private business college and normal school in Concordia, Kansas; founded 1889. Records show students as late as 1930; operations later moved to Webb City, Missouri. Closure year and cause not stated in the cited source.

name: Kansas Christian College (Lincoln)
notes: Christian college in Lincoln, Kansas; established 1882, classes from 1885, closed 1913. Distinct from the still-open Kansas Christian College in Overland Park. Source states no cause.

name: Kansas City University (1896-1933)
notes: Methodist university in Kansas City, Kansas; the successor-in-interest to Campbell College. Ceased operations 1933. Distinct from the still-open Kansas City University in Missouri. Source states no cause.

name: Kansas Technical Institute
notes: State two-year technical college (originally Schilling Institute) on the former Schilling Air Force Base; founded 1965. Became a campus of Kansas State University in 1991 (now K-State Salina).

name: Lane University
notes: United Brethren university in Lecompton, Kansas; founded 1865. United with Campbell University in 1902 to form Campbell College, which itself closed in 1933. Source states no cause.

name: Leavenworth Normal School
notes: Kansas state normal school (teacher training); founded May 3, 1870. Closed 1876 when the state consolidated its normal schools under the Miscellaneous appropriations bill of 1876.

name: Miltonvale Wesleyan College
notes: Wesleyan Church college in Miltonvale, Kansas; began operation 1909. Merged in 1972 with Bartlesville Wesleyan College, later part of Oklahoma Wesleyan University. Source states no cause.

name: Salina Normal University
notes: Independent normal university in Salina, Kansas offering collegiate, normal, business, science and fine-arts courses; founded 1884. Destroyed by fire September 4, 1904 and not rebuilt.
motto: Study first, outside issues afterwards.

name: Utopia College
notes: Two-year college in Eureka, Kansas founded 1946 by Roger Babson to teach practical business; renamed Midwest Institute of Business Administration in 1955. Closed 1970 amid declining enrollment.

name: Hahnemann Medical College of the Pacific
notes: Homeopathic medical college in San Francisco; founded 1881. Merged with the University of California medical school (today UCSF) in 1915, consummated July 1, 1918. Distinct from the Hahnemann medical colleges in Pennsylvania.

name: Indiana Medical College
notes: Proprietary medical college in Indianapolis; founded 1869. Merged in 1905 into Purdue's medical school and folded into the Indiana University School of Medicine by 1908.

name: New Orleans School of Medicine
notes: Proprietary medical school in New Orleans; founded 1856. Closed for the Civil War in 1862, reopened 1866, and finally closed in 1870. No surviving successor.

name: Berkshire Medical College
notes: Medical college in Pittsfield, Massachusetts; began 1823 as the Medical Department of Williams College and was disbanded in 1867 with no surviving medical successor. Source states no cause.

name: Touro University College of Medicine
notes: Medical school of the Touro College and University System, chartered 2007 in Hackensack, New Jersey; disbanded December 2009 before opening. The system instead acquired the still-operating New York Medical College. Distinct from the operating Touro University campuses.
motto: Advancing health care through science, compassion and caring.

name: Atlantic School of Osteopathy
notes: Osteopathic school in Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania; founded 1898. Merged by 1906 into the American School of Osteopathy (now A.T. Still University) amid regulatory trouble over diplomas.

name: Toledo Medical College
notes: Medical college in Toledo, Ohio, operating 1882 to 1914. No surviving successor named in the source, which also does not state a cause. Control inferred from its proprietary funding.

name: Penn Medical University
notes: Eclectic proprietary medical school in Philadelphia, founded 1853 as Penn Medical College and renamed 1854; closed 1881. Not the University of Pennsylvania. Source states no cause; control inferred from its proprietary form.

name: Chattanooga Medical College
notes: Medical department of U.S. Grant University (later the University of Chattanooga, now the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga); founded 1889. The parent closed the medical college in 1910 to focus on undergraduate accreditation; no surviving medical successor.

name: University of West Tennessee College of Medicine and Surgery
notes: Historically Black proprietary medical college founded 1900 in Jackson, Tennessee by Miles V. Lynk and Beebe Steven Lynk; moved to Memphis in 1907. Closed 1923, largely due to the Flexner Report.

name: Fort Worth University
notes: Methodist Episcopal general university in Fort Worth, Texas; chartered 1881. Merged in 1911 with the Methodist University of Oklahoma, now Oklahoma City University. Source states no cause.

name: Grenada College
notes: Church-run women's college in Grenada, Mississippi; founded 1850 (Baptist, later Methodist). Closed 1936 on financial troubles, its assets transferred to Millsaps College.

name: Asheville Female College
notes: Methodist women's college, the first institution of higher education in western North Carolina; active 1841 to 1901. Source states no cause.

name: Boscobel College
notes: Baptist women's college in Nashville, founded 1889 as the Nashville Baptist Female College. Closed 1916 on account of the East Nashville fire.

name: Hamilton College (Kentucky)
notes: Women's college in Lexington, Kentucky, founded 1869. Taken over by Transylvania University in 1903 and run as an affiliated junior college until it closed during the Great Depression in 1932.

name: Hartford College for Women
notes: Two-year women's college in Hartford, opened 1933. Became a constituent college of the University of Hartford in 1991 and was dissolved into its College of Arts and Sciences in 2003.
motto: Sibi constantem esse: to be true to oneself

name: Hillman College
notes: Baptist women's college in Clinton, Mississippi, founded 1853 as the Central Female Institute and renamed Hillman College in 1891. Purchased and absorbed by Mississippi College in 1942. Source states no cause.

name: Pleasant J. Potter College
notes: Private women's college in Bowling Green, Kentucky; operated 1889 to 1909. Closed May 20, 1909 amid financial difficulty; its campus was later bought by the predecessor of Western Kentucky University, a real-estate purchase rather than a merger.

name: Oxford College for Women
notes: Presbyterian women's college in Oxford, Ohio, formed 1867. After continued financial distress, Miami University took over ownership in 1928 and absorbed its students.

name: Ottumwa Heights College
notes: Catholic women's college (coeducational from 1967) in Ottumwa, Iowa, founded 1864 as Visitation Academy. Merged with Indian Hills Community College in 1979. Source states no cause.

name: Kidd-Key College
notes: Methodist women's college and conservatory of music in Sherman, Texas, founded 1877 as North Texas Female College and renamed Kidd-Key College in 1919. Closed June 1935 amid declining enrollment and the Depression.

name: Campbell-Hagerman College
notes: Disciples of Christ women's college in Lexington, Kentucky, founded 1903. Discontinued in 1912 following the death of co-founder Mary Anna Campbell Hagerman, who directed the school.

name: Carolina College (Maxton, North Carolina)
notes: Methodist women's college in Maxton, North Carolina, founded 1912 (a junior college from 1919). Financial difficulties forced its closure in 1926.
motto: We can and we will

name: Carr-Burdette College
notes: Disciples of Christ women's school in Sherman, Texas, founded 1894, run as a preparatory school and junior college. Closed 1929. Source states no cause.

name: Chickasaw Female College
notes: Women's college in Pontotoc, Mississippi, founded 1851 and run by the Presbyterian Church from 1853; closed 1936. The source calls it a women's college but gives no grade levels; postsecondary standing rests on that wording. Source states no cause.

name: Littleton Female College
notes: Methodist women's college in Littleton, North Carolina, operating 1882 to 1919; destroyed by fire in 1919.

name: Long College for Women
notes: Presbyterian women's college established 1947 as a coordinate of Hanover College in Hanover, Indiana. Merged into Hanover College in 1978 amid financial pressure after 1974 tornado damage and the shift to coeducation.

name: Lynnland Female Institute
notes: Private women's liberal arts college in Glendale, Kentucky (despite the 'Institute' name), chartered 1867. Closed June 23, 1915 when the campus was sold to the Kentucky Baptist Children's Home for use as an orphanage.

name: Saint Joseph College of Florida
notes: Catholic college run by the Sisters of St. Joseph of Florida (St. Augustine, then Jensen Beach); a two-year junior college from 1957, coeducational from 1966. Closed May 1972; the Jensen Beach campus passed to the Florida Institute of Technology.

name: Sinsinawa Mound College
notes: Catholic men's college on Sinsinawa Mound, Wisconsin, founded 1846 by Samuel Mazzuchelli; sold in 1852. Distinct from the later Dominican women's college and academy on the same site. Source states no cause.

name: Evelyn College for Women
notes: Coordinate women's college associated with Princeton, founded 1887. Fell on hard times after the Panic of 1893 and closed permanently in 1897; it did not merge into Princeton.

name: Evanston College for Ladies
notes: Women's college in Evanston, Illinois, founded 1871 with Frances Willard as first president. After the Great Chicago Fire left its donors unable to pay, it merged into Northwestern University in 1873 as the Woman's College of Northwestern.

name: Englewood Cliffs College
notes: Catholic two-year women's college in Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey, founded 1962 by the Sisters of St. Joseph of Newark. Closed June 7, 1974 for financial reasons; its campus was later acquired by St. Peter's College.
motto: Quis Ut Deus: Who is like God?

name: Thomas More College (New York City)
notes: The women's coordinate college of Fordham University at Rose Hill, founded 1964. Merged into Fordham College at Rose Hill in 1974 when that college became coeducational.

name: Marymount California University
notes: Catholic university founded 1932 (a junior college until 1947) by the Religious of the Sacred Heart of Mary. Closed August 1, 2022 after a planned merger with Saint Leo University fell through; UCLA bought the campus.
motto: Tua Luce Dirige: Direct Us by Thy Light

name: Mary Sharp College
notes: Baptist women's college in Winchester, Tennessee, founded 1851, noted as the first women's college to offer degrees equivalent to men's colleges. Closed 1896 amid the economic depression of the 1890s.

name: Due West Female College
notes: Associate Reformed Presbyterian women's college in Due West, South Carolina, founded 1859. Merged into Erskine College in 1927 (officially closed 1928) after Erskine became coeducational.

name: Mary Allen Seminary
notes: Historically Black Presbyterian school in Crockett, Texas, founded 1886 for freedwomen; an accredited junior college from 1932 and coeducational from 1933. Closed 1972 (also briefly closed 1943 to 1944). Source states no cause for the final closure.

name: Clinton College (Kentucky)
notes: Baptist college in Clinton, Kentucky, offering instruction from primary to collegiate levels; established 1874 as Clinton Female College, coeducational from 1876. Closed 1915. Distinct from the still-open Clinton College in South Carolina. Source states no cause.

name: Chicora College
notes: Presbyterian women's college in South Carolina (Greenville, then Columbia), founded 1893. Merged March 24, 1930 into Queens College, Charlotte, now Queens University of Charlotte.
motto: Non ministrari sed ministrare: Not to be served, but to serve

name: Coates College for Women
notes: Women's liberal arts college in Terre Haute, Indiana, founded 1885 by Jane B. Coates. Closed 1897 after Coates's death removed its funding, compounded by the Panic of 1893.

name: Flora MacDonald College
notes: Presbyterian women's college in Red Springs, North Carolina, founded 1896 as Red Springs Seminary. Merged in 1961 with Presbyterian Junior College to form St. Andrews Presbyterian College; that successor (later St. Andrews University) itself closed in May 2025.

name: San Diego College for Women
notes: Catholic women's college founded 1950 by the Society of the Sacred Heart. Merged in 1972 with the San Diego College for Men to form the University of San Diego.

name: Ward-Belmont College
notes: Nashville junior college and conservatory formed in 1913 from Ward Seminary (1865) and Belmont College (1890). In 1951 its college division was sold to the Tennessee Baptist Convention and became Belmont College, now Belmont University; its prep division became Harpeth Hall School.

name: Western College for Women
notes: Liberal arts women's college in Oxford, Ohio, founded 1853 as a daughter school of Mount Holyoke and a host of Freedom Summer training in 1964. Merged into Miami University in 1974 (now its Western Campus).

name: Mundelein College
notes: Catholic women's liberal arts college in Chicago, founded 1930 by the Sisters of Charity of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Enrollment fell sharply in the 1980s; affiliated with and absorbed into Loyola University Chicago in 1991.

name: Mount Saint Mary College (New Hampshire)
notes: Catholic women's college in Hooksett, New Hampshire, run by the Sisters of Mercy; a college from 1934 (an academy from 1893). Closed May 1978 amid declining enrollment and the move away from single-sex education. Distinct from the operating Mount Saint Mary colleges elsewhere.

name: Greenbrier College
notes: Women's college in Lewisburg, West Virginia, tracing to the 1812 Lewisburg Academy. Closed 1972 and sold to the state. Source states no cause.

name: Forest Park University
notes: Women's college in the St. Louis area, founded 1861 as Kirkwood Seminary and a four-year college from 1886; closed 1925. Source states no cause.

name: Mount Sacred Heart College
notes: Catholic junior college in Hamden, Connecticut, founded 1946 by the Apostles of the Sacred Heart of Jesus. Closed mid-1997 amid low enrollment.

name: Barrington College
notes: Evangelical Christian liberal arts college in Barrington, Rhode Island, founded 1900. Merged into the still-operating Gordon College in Wenham, Massachusetts, in 1985.

name: Litchfield Law School
notes: The first independent law school in America, founded 1774 by Tapping Reeve and unaffiliated with any college; closed 1833. Source states no cause.

name: Winchester Law School
notes: Independent law school in Winchester, Virginia, founded 1824 by Henry St. George Tucker Sr., who closed it in 1831 after his election to the Virginia Court of Appeals required moving to Richmond.

name: Staunton Law School
notes: Independent law school in Staunton, Virginia, founded 1831; closed 1849 amid competition from other schools.

name: Northampton Law School
notes: Independent law school in Northampton, Massachusetts, opened 1823 by Judge Samuel Howe on the Litchfield model. Closed 1829 when its leader John Ashmun left for a Harvard Law professorship; students dispersed to Harvard.

name: Atlanta Law School
notes: Independent law school in Atlanta, founded 1890 (originally the legal department of Southern Medical School). Closed 1994 after Georgia limited the bar exam to ABA-accredited graduates.

name: Augusta Law School
notes: The first law school in Georgia, founded 1833 in Augusta. A first iteration closed 1854; a second operated into the 1980s. Exact closure year and cause not given in the source.

name: Terrell Law School
notes: The Robert H. Terrell Law School, a historically Black law school in Washington, D.C., founded 1931. Closed 1950 as other law schools integrated and removed its niche.

name: Woodrow Wilson College of Law
notes: Independent night law school in Atlanta, founded 1933; closed 1989 after failing to obtain ABA accreditation. A Georgia State University takeover proposed in 1981 was never completed.

name: Lincoln College of Law
notes: Independent law college in Springfield, Illinois, operating 1911 to 1953. Source states neither control nor cause.

name: Milwaukee Law School
notes: Independent law school in Milwaukee, founded 1892 as the Milwaukee Law Class. In 1908 it was acquired, with the Milwaukee University Law School, to become the core of Marquette University Law School. Source states no cause.

name: Chattanooga College of Law
notes: Law school in Chattanooga, founded 1898 as the law department of Grant University (later the University of Chattanooga, now UT Chattanooga). Closed 1942 as admission standards rose; the source does not resolve whether it was still part of the university at closure.

name: Alben W. Barkley School of Law
notes: For-profit law school in Paducah, Kentucky, founded 2004 as the American Justice School of Law and renamed in 2008. Never ABA-accredited; filed bankruptcy and closed December 31, 2008.

name: Nevada School of Law at Old College
notes: Unaccredited law school in Reno, Nevada, founded 1981; closed August 1988 lacking the means to gain ABA accreditation.

name: Northern Virginia Law School
notes: Weekend law school founded in the late 1970s as the District of Columbia Law School, moved to Alexandria, Virginia in 1980; closed in the 1990s after failing to gain full accreditation. Source gives no control and no exact years.

name: Concordia University School of Law
notes: Law school in Boise, Idaho, founded 2011 under Concordia University (Portland). Closed after summer 2020 when its parent closed and a transfer to Concordia University-St. Paul could not be finalized.

name: Valparaiso University School of Law
notes: Law school of the still-operating Valparaiso University (Indiana), founded 1879. Suspended admissions in 2017 after a 2016 ABA censure over admissions practices; last class graduated 2020.

name: South Carolina State University School of Law
notes: Historically Black law school of the still-operating South Carolina State University, founded 1947. Enrollment collapsed after the University of South Carolina began admitting Black students in 1964; closed June 1966.

name: Lincoln University School of Law
notes: Law school of the still-operating Lincoln University of Missouri (a public HBCU), founded 1939. Enrollment fell to 12 by 1954 and the school closed as a drain on university resources; students folded into the University of Missouri School of Law.

name: Hamline University School of Law
notes: Law school of the still-operating Hamline University, founded 1972. Merged December 9, 2015 with William Mitchell College of Law to form Mitchell Hamline School of Law.

name: William Mitchell College of Law
notes: Independent law school in St. Paul, founded 1900 as the St. Paul College of Law and named for William Mitchell in 1956. Merged with Hamline University School of Law in 2015 to form Mitchell Hamline School of Law.
motto: Practical Wisdom

name: Hartford College of Law
notes: Independent law school in Hartford, founded 1921. After a 1943 trial period the University of Connecticut absorbed it in 1948 as the still-operating UConn School of Law.

name: National University School of Law
notes: Law school of National University in Washington, D.C., founded 1869. Declining enrollment led to a 1954 merger into the still-operating George Washington University Law School.

name: Bryson College
notes: College in Fayetteville, Tennessee, operating 1919 to 1929. Source is a stub; control inferred and no cause stated.

name: Columbus College (South Dakota)
notes: Catholic men's school (prep, high school and college) founded 1909 in Chamberlain, South Dakota, by the Diocese of Sioux Falls; relocated to Sioux Falls in 1921. Closed August 1929 amid the farm economy's collapse.

name: Des Moines University (1865-1929)
notes: Baptist university in Des Moines, founded 1865; closed September 1929 following court action arising from campus unrest under the Baptist Bible Union. Distinct from the still-operating osteopathic Des Moines University.

name: Texas Presbyterian College
notes: Cumberland Presbyterian women's college in Milford, Texas, founded 1902 and fully accredited from 1917. Merged into the still-operating Austin College in 1929.

name: Spokane College
notes: Norwegian Lutheran liberal arts college in Spokane, Washington (with a law school), founded 1906. Merged in 1929 into what is now the still-operating Pacific Lutheran University. Source states no cause.

name: Roger Williams University (Tennessee)
notes: Historically Black Baptist university in Nashville, founded 1866. After fires and Depression-era financial trouble it was absorbed into the Howe Institute in Memphis, now the still-operating LeMoyne-Owen College.

name: Jonesboro College
notes: Baptist liberal arts junior college in Jonesboro, Arkansas, founded 1924; closed 1934 amid financial trouble, its buildings taken over by the local school district.

name: Will Mayfield College
notes: Baptist junior college in Marble Hill, Missouri, founded 1878 as Mayfield-Smith Academy and renamed 1903; offered four years of preparatory and two of junior-college work. Closed 1934.

name: Concordia College (North Carolina)
notes: Lutheran high school and junior college in Conover, North Carolina, founded 1878. An April 1935 fire destroyed the administration building and the Missouri Synod declined to rebuild; it closed that spring.

name: DeLancey Divinity School
notes: Episcopal Church seminary in Geneva and Buffalo, New York, founded 1850; closed in 1935 by Bishop Cameron J. Davis.

name: Dixie University
notes: Short-lived university in Dallas, Texas, founded 1933 out of the Somerville Law School; closed permanently by 1935. Not related to Utah's Dixie State University.

name: New Orleans University
notes: Historically Black Methodist university in New Orleans, founded 1869 by the Freedmen's Aid Society. Consolidated in 1935 with Straight College to form the still-operating Dillard University.

name: The Beethoven Conservatory
notes: Music conservatory in St. Louis, founded 1871; closed 1936 during the Great Depression.

name: Bowdon College
notes: Coeducational college in Bowdon, Georgia, chartered 1857; under University of Georgia governance 1919 to 1933, then a private junior college. Closed 1936 amid Depression-era financial trouble.

name: Mound Bayou Industrial College
notes: Historically Black Baptist college in Mound Bayou, Mississippi, founded 1900 and financed by the women of the General Baptist Convention; closed 1936. Source states no cause.

name: Guadalupe College
notes: Historically Black Baptist college in Seguin, Texas, founded 1884. A February 1936 fire destroyed the main building and the rebuilding drive was cancelled in 1937, ending the school.

name: Cleveland Institute of Electronics
notes: For-profit technical/correspondence school in Cleveland, founded 1934; closed September 30, 2022. Source states no cause.
motto: A School of thousands. A class of one. Since 1934.

name: Lutheran School of Nursing
notes: Hospital-affiliated diploma nursing school in St. Louis, founded 1898; closed permanently July 27, 2022 after its hospital's bankruptcy.

name: Washington Technology University
notes: For-profit university in Bellevue, Washington, founded 2017; shut down July 29, 2022 after the state denied renewal of its authorization to operate.
motto: Grow, Explore, Learn

name: University of the Sciences
notes: Philadelphia university founded 1821 as the Philadelphia College of Pharmacy. After enrollment decline and deficits it merged into the still-operating Saint Joseph's University on June 1, 2022.
motto: Nosse haec omnia salus est: To know all this is health

name: SS. Cyril and Methodius Seminary
notes: Polish Roman Catholic seminary founded 1885 in Detroit, at Orchard Lake, Michigan from 1909; closed 2022. Its parent, Orchard Lake Schools, still operates. Source states no cause.

name: Southwest University of Visual Arts
notes: For-profit art and design college in Tucson, Arizona (formerly The Art Center Design College), founded 1983; closed November 2020. Source states no cause.

name: California International Business University
notes: For-profit university in San Diego founded 1995; closed May 2020, attributed to the COVID-19 pandemic.

name: Robert Morris University Illinois
notes: Chicago university founded 1965 (roots in the 1913 Moser School). Merged in 2020 into the still-operating Roosevelt University, which formed a Robert Morris Experiential College.

name: Lindenwood University - Belleville
notes: Belleville, Illinois branch campus of the still-operating Lindenwood University (St. Charles, Missouri), opened as a four-year institution in 2009. Undergraduate programs ended after 2019-20 amid financial and enrollment pressure; students could transfer to St. Charles.

name: Castleton University
notes: Public university in Castleton, Vermont, chartered 1787. Consolidated in July 2023 with Northern Vermont University and Vermont Technical College to form the still-operating Vermont State University, of which it is now a branch campus.

name: University of Wisconsin-Platteville Richland
notes: Two-year branch campus of the still-operating University of Wisconsin-Platteville, founded 1967. In-person instruction ended May 2023 (campus officially closed July 1, 2023) after enrollment fell to 64.

name: Art Institute of Tampa
notes: For-profit art school in Tampa, Florida, opened 2004 as the 30th location of The Art Institutes system; closed September 30, 2023 in the systemwide shutdown. Source states no cause.

name: Granite State College
notes: Public adult-focused college of the University System of New Hampshire, founded 1972. Merged in 2023 into the still-operating University of New Hampshire as its College of Professional Studies. Source states no cause.

name: New Hampshire Institute of Art
notes: Art college in Manchester, New Hampshire, founded 1898. Merged in 2019 into the still-operating New England College; the Manchester campus was later closed by New England College in 2023. Source states no cause.

name: Apollos University
notes: Small for-profit university in Great Falls, Montana, founded 2004; closed December 2024. Source states no cause.
motto: The Gateway to Your Future

name: University of Wisconsin-Oshkosh, Fond du Lac Campus
notes: Two-year branch of the still-operating University of Wisconsin-Oshkosh, founded 1968; final class May 17, 2024 amid the statewide cut of regional campuses.

name: University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee at Washington County
notes: Two-year regional campus of the still-operating University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, founded 1968; closed June 30, 2024 amid declining enrollment.

name: People's College of Law
notes: Unaccredited, all-volunteer social-justice law school in Los Angeles, founded 1974; its degree-granting authority was terminated May 31, 2024 after years of State Bar probation and financial strain.
motto: Producing Social Justice Lawyers

name: John Witherspoon College
notes: Christian liberal-arts college in Rapid City, South Dakota, restructured under this name in 2011 (from the 2007 Black Hills Bible Institute); closed May 2024 for lack of funding.
motto: Fides Quaerens Intellectum: Faith Seeking Understanding

name: Fairfax University of America
notes: University in Fairfax, Virginia, founded 1998; ceased operations December 31, 2024, citing a complex regulatory environment and too little time to secure new accreditation.

name: Baptist Theological Seminary at Richmond
notes: Free-standing moderate Baptist seminary in Richmond, Virginia, founded 1989; closed effective June 30, 2019, the trustees citing financial pressure.

name: Washington Theological Union
notes: Catholic graduate seminary in Washington, D.C., founded 1968 by the Franciscan, Carmelite and Augustinian orders; ceased operations June 30, 2015 amid low enrollment and declining vocations.
motto: freedom, faith, integrity

name: University of Texas at Brownsville
parent_name: University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
notes: Public university in Brownsville, Texas, founded 1991. Dissolved August 31, 2015 and merged with the University of Texas-Pan American to form the still-operating University of Texas Rio Grande Valley.

name: University of Texas-Pan American
parent_name: University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
notes: Public university in Edinburg, Texas, founded 1927. Dissolved August 31, 2015 and merged with the University of Texas at Brownsville to form the still-operating University of Texas Rio Grande Valley.

name: Tennessee Temple University
notes: Independent Baptist university in Chattanooga, founded 1946; merged April 30, 2015 into the still-operating Piedmont International University. Source states no cause.
motto: Training to Transform

name: Drexel University Sacramento
notes: Sacramento satellite campus of the still-operating Drexel University (Philadelphia), opened 2009; began closing in spring 2015. Some graduate programs moved to the University of the Pacific. Source states no cause.

name: IADT Tampa
notes: Tampa campus (opened 1984) of the International Academy of Design and Technology, a Career Education Corporation chain; rebranded Sanford-Brown in 2014 and closed 2015. Source states no cause.

name: Heald College
notes: Closure recorded on collegeevaluator.com; no IPEDS name match (school likely closed before 2004, IPEDS HD's start). No federal OPEID (absent from IPEDS/SHEEO/PEPS).

name: AIB College of Business
notes: Business college in Des Moines, Iowa, founded 1921; closed June 30, 2016 after 95 years, gifting its campus to the state. Source states no cause.
motto: Ethical, productive, and engaged citizens.

name: American Sports University
notes: Unaccredited university in San Bernardino, California, founded 2006; closed 2016 when the state denied renewal of its license. Source does not state for-profit vs nonprofit.

name: Darton State College
notes: Public college in Albany, Georgia, founded 1963 as Albany Junior College; consolidated in 2016 into the still-operating Albany State University (now its West Campus).
motto: A Better Beginning

name: George Wythe University
notes: Unaccredited university in Salt Lake City, founded 1992; the Utah Division of Consumer Protection ordered it to close in August 2016.
motto: Building Statesmen

name: Michigan Jewish Institute
notes: Chabad-affiliated college in West Bloomfield, Michigan, founded 1994; closed 2016 after the Dept. of Education denied recertification and federal aid access.

name: St. Catharine College
notes: Catholic college near Springfield, Kentucky, founded 1931 by the Dominican Sisters; closed July 2016 under a $5 million deficit and a federal student-aid dispute.

name: McNally Smith College of Music
notes: Independent music college in St. Paul, founded 1984; declared bankruptcy December 17 and closed December 20, 2017.

name: Lutheran Theological Seminary at Gettysburg
notes: Lutheran seminary in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, founded 1826; merged July 1, 2017 with the Lutheran Theological Seminary at Philadelphia to form the still-operating United Lutheran Seminary.

name: Le Cordon Bleu Institute of Culinary Arts - Dallas
notes: Dallas culinary school of the Career Education Corporation Le Cordon Bleu chain; closed 2017 in the systemwide wind-down. The source gives a contradictory founding year (1999 vs 2007), so none is recorded.

name: Culinard
notes: Culinary school founded 2000 as the culinary division of Virginia College (Education Corporation of America), with campuses in Alabama and the Southeast; closed December 2018 in the ECA shutdown.

name: Coleman University
notes: Technology university in San Diego, founded 1963; closed August 2018. Its nonprofit status and an accreditation/conversion bid were contested near closure, so control is recorded per Wikipedia and should be confirmed against IPEDS.
motto: Aspirationes in realitatem: Dreams Into Reality

name: Armstrong State University
notes: Public university in Savannah, Georgia, founded 1935 as Armstrong Junior College; consolidated into the still-operating Georgia Southern University on January 17, 2018 as its Armstrong Campus.

name: Lyndon State College
notes: Public college in Lyndonville, Vermont, founded 1911; merged July 1, 2018 with Johnson State College to form Northern Vermont University, later consolidated into the still-operating Vermont State University.
motto: Ad Illuminandum Regnum: Toward a Brightening Kingdom

name: International Academy of Design and Technology San Antonio
notes: San Antonio campus of the Career Education Corporation IADT chain, founded 2005; placed in teach-out in 2015 and closed January 12, 2018. Peak enrollment about 400 full-time students.

name: Institute for Advanced Study of Human Sexuality
notes: Graduate school of sexology in San Francisco, founded 1976; closed 2018 after California declined to renew its degree-granting approval in 2016 and it did not obtain accreditation.

name: Silicon Valley University
notes: Graduate university in San Jose, California, founded 1997; California regulators ordered it to close April 5, 2018 after it lost accreditation. Control recorded per Wikipedia (nonprofit) and should be confirmed against IPEDS.
motto: University Caters To Silicon Valley

name: Solex College
notes: For-profit college in the Chicago area, founded 1995; closed 2018. Peak enrollment over 2,000 in 2013-2014. Source states no cause; a 2015 Title IV audit was dismissed in 2018.
motto: Learn Today. Earn Tomorrow.

name: Northwest Theological Seminary
notes: Reformed seminary in Lynnwood, Washington, founded 2000; closed 2018. Source states no cause.
motto: His Story is our story

name: Berean Institute
notes: Historically Black vocational school in Philadelphia, founded 1899 by Rev. Matthew Anderson to teach skilled trades; evicted from its state-owned building and closed in 2012.

name: University of Northern Virginia
notes: For-profit university in Annandale, Virginia, founded 1998; peaked around 2,400 students (~90% from India). Virginia revoked its license in 2013 for lack of recognized accreditation and it wound down in 2014.

name: National Labor College
notes: AFL-CIO-affiliated college in Silver Spring, Maryland, founded 1969 (degree-granting from 1997); closed April 26, 2014 under roughly $30 million of debt after a campus sale fell through.

name: Willamette University School of Education
notes: Graduate teacher-education school of the still-operating Willamette University, founded 1988; closed May 2014 amid financial pressure and a weak teacher market.

name: College of Saints John Fisher and Thomas More
notes: Traditionalist Catholic college in Fort Worth, Texas, founded 1981; closed 2014 after a dispute over the Latin Mass on campus alongside financial and enrollment decline (about 25 students by spring 2014).
motto: Deum Cognoscere Diligere Servire: To Know, To Love, and To Serve God

name: Augusta State University
notes: Public university in Augusta, Georgia, tracing to a 1925 junior college; consolidated in 2013 with Georgia Health Sciences University to form what is now the still-operating Augusta University.

name: Gainesville State College
notes: Public college in Oakwood, Georgia, founded 1964; consolidated in 2013 with North Georgia College & State University to form the still-operating University of North Georgia.
motto: Student Focused, Learning Centered

name: Middle Georgia College
notes: Public college in Cochran, Georgia, founded 1884; consolidated in 2013 with Macon State College to form the still-operating Middle Georgia State University.

name: Middle Georgia Technical College
notes: Public technical college in Warner Robins, Georgia, founded 1973; merged July 1, 2013 into the still-operating Central Georgia Technical College.

name: Southern Polytechnic State University
notes: Public polytechnic university in Marietta, Georgia, founded 1948; consolidated July 1, 2015 into the still-operating Kennesaw State University as its college of engineering.
motto: Imagination, Innovation, Application

name: Elizabeth Seton College
notes: Catholic junior college in Yonkers, New York, founded 1961 by the Sisters of Charity; merged into the still-operating Iona College in 1989 (its Seton campus closed 1995). Enrollment ~980 in 1988.

name: Natchez Junior College
notes: Historically Black Baptist junior college in Natchez, Mississippi, founded 1884; closed 1989. Source states no cause.

name: Prentiss Institute
notes: Historically Black school in Prentiss, Mississippi, founded 1907 with Rosenwald support; its junior college ran until 1989. Enrollment about 700 in 1957.

name: Worcester Junior College
notes: Nonprofit junior college in Worcester, Massachusetts, founded 1905 as the Worcester YMCA Institute; foreclosed and closed April 21, 1989.

name: The World University (Puerto Rico)
notes: Middle States-accredited university in Puerto Rico (Ponce, Hato Rey, Bayamon), founded 1965; closed 1989. Source does not state control or cause. Distinct from a same-named school in Arizona.

name: Combs College of Music
notes: Music conservatory in Philadelphia, founded 1885 as the Combs Broad Street Conservatory; closed 1990 amid financial hardship and an inadequate endowment.

name: Georgetown University School of Dentistry
notes: Dental school of the still-operating Georgetown University, founded 1901; the university decided in 1987 to close it and the last class graduated in 1990 amid a projected multimillion-dollar deficit.

name: American Conservatory of Music
notes: Music conservatory in Chicago, founded 1886; enrollment fell from a 1931 peak of about 3,000 to 90 full-time students, and it closed in bankruptcy in 1991. Distinct from the American Conservatory Theater in San Francisco.

name: Washington University School of Dental Medicine
notes: Dental school of the still-operating Washington University in St. Louis, founded 1866 (the first west of the Mississippi); the board voted to close it in 1989 and it closed in 1991 amid deficits and state-school competition.

name: Columbia University School of Library Service
notes: The first US library school, at the still-operating Columbia University, founded 1887; closed June 30, 1992 in a university budget crisis. Peak enrollment 1,071 in 1938-39.

name: Edmondson Junior College
notes: For-profit junior college in Chattanooga, Tennessee, owned by Phillips College, Inc.; closed July 1992 amid a federal fraud case. Source states no founding year or cause.

name: Hawaii Loa College
notes: Liberal-arts college in Kaneohe, Hawaii, founded 1963; facing loss of accreditation and $3 million in debt, it merged in 1992 into the still-operating Hawaii Pacific University.
motto: A'ole i kaupo'o ana no: My height is not yet reached

name: Illinois Technical College
notes: Electronics trade college in downtown Chicago, founded 1950 as the Chicago School of Television Repair; closed 1992. Source states neither control nor cause.

name: McKenzie College (Tennessee)
notes: Proprietary business college in Chattanooga, Tennessee, founded 1885; closed 1992. Source states no cause.

name: Nazareth College (Michigan)
notes: Catholic liberal-arts college in Kalamazoo, Michigan, founded 1914 by the Sisters of St. Joseph of Nazareth; announced closure in 1991 and phased out over 18 months, closing 1992. Source states no cause.

name: Tarkio College
notes: Presbyterian liberal-arts college in Tarkio, Missouri, founded 1883; closed 1992 after filing for bankruptcy in 1991.

name: University of Minnesota Waseca
notes: Two-year technical college campus of the still-operating University of Minnesota, opened 1971; closed 1992, the site later becoming a federal prison and a research center. Source states no cause.

name: World College West
notes: Liberal-arts college in Marin County, California, founded 1973; closed in fall 1992 after a leadership-succession failure left it about $4 million in debt.
